newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Noise curbs to cost Schiphol dear - airport chief. [CORRECTED 13:44 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Noise curbs to cost Schiphol dear - airport chief. [CORRECTED 13:44 GMT]

text.p: Tough new restrictions on night flights out of Schiphol could cost Amsterdam's airport several thousand jobs and up to 10 percent of its freight volume, Schiphol president Hans Smits said on Friday.
"(The measures) will seriously jeopardise five to 10 percent of cargo volume and we could lose it," Smits told a news conference.

The restrictions, aimed at keeping noise levels within legally determined limits, will ban night-time take-offs of most wide-body aircraft -- such as DC10s and Boeing 747 100s,200s and 300s and the Boeing 747SP -- from August 1.
The night ban -- valid from 2300 through 0600 hours -- will also apply to all non-scheduled flights, Smits said.
This means that scheduled flights running into delays which reach beyond the 2300 watershed will not be allowed to take off, he said.
The restrictions will particularly affect cargo carriers operating through Schiphol and, to a lesser extent, charter airlines, Smits said.
Schiphol is expected to lose (corrects from 'handle') some 30,000 tonnes of cargo this year, rising to 50-100,000 in 1998.

The loss of freight volume resulting from the night-flight ban will lead to job losses throughout the industry chain, with handling company Aero Ground Services likely to be hit particularly hard, Smits said.

Israel's El Al and privately-owned Polar Air will be severely affected by the measures, as well as Dutch freight and passenger charter airline Martinair, KLM's 50-50 freight and passenger joint venture with Rotterdam-based Nedlloyd.

Both El Al and Polar Air had contributed "very constructively" in talks offering to reschedule a number of flights to daylight hours, but this would not in itself be enough to resolve the problem, Smits said.
KLM, Schiphol's heaviest user, had indicated its fleet mix will enable it to cope with the restrictions without undue disruption, Smits said.
But El Al is now mulling the transfer of its cargo hub to Belgium's Liege airport, and Martinair has slammed the proposed measures as discriminatory and unfair.
"The three Boeing 747 aircraft operated by Martinair are so-called chapter three aircraft...of the most low-noise," it said in a statement.
"Excluding Martinair chapter three aircraft while allowing aircraft from other airlines which fall into the same category is unreasonable and, in Martinair's view, unacceptable," the airline said.
Martinair said its night-time flight movements had remained constant over the last three years and as such it had not contributed to the capacity bottleneck.

But Smits said Schiphol's failure to agree a voluntary 50 percent reduction in night-time take-offs with the airlines concerned meant it had been forced to impose a unilateral ban which affected the culpable and non-culpable alike.
Some 70 percent of Schiphol's annual quota of night flights had already been used up, Smits said.
This was due mainly to greater-than-envisaged deployment of noisy wide-body aircraft and the use of Hercules craft for charter and freight, he said.
"If we don't impose these restrictions now, the whole airport would have to be shut overnight from around September," Smits said.

He said Schiphol had requested urgent talks with transport minister Annemarie Jorritsma in a bid to resolve the problem of noise restrictions which will effectively limit further airport growth to "a few percent" over the coming years.
